body.title: Academic Integrity and Credibility
body.body:
Academic integrity is vital to the credibility of a student, a program and a university

A university lives by its reputation. It is always evaluated based on the reputation that has been built over the years through its collective accomplishments. Specifically, the reputation of the university is a weighted sum of the reputation of all of its past and present members (students, faculty and staff). The reputation of a university helps it to attract its future faculty and students as well as financial donations in order for it to continue in its mission. Hence, the reputation of the university is a critical asset that it needs to safeguard, maintain, and improve.

A university gains visibility, be it positive or negative, through either its accomplishments or mishaps. One person’s actions will positively or negatively affect the reputation of the program, department, school and university they belong to. Furthermore, every member of the university community will represent the university name even after they leave the university. Hence, their actions will always be connected to their university. It is the responsibility of every member of the community to foster a culture of high integrity which leads to positive visibility and improves reputation. Taking any form of shortcut in any academic task, such as assignment, project, exam, paper, research study, etc., will ruin a university’s reputation. For example, a student’s short-term benefits in grades due to cheating will eventually be unmasked through future professional interaction. With that said, a student who chooses to commit an academic integrity violation (AIV) will adversely impact the student and university's reputation.

When you join a university to participate in its academic and scholarship activities, you are not only a student, but also a member of the world-wide scientific community. You will be our colleague, and your work will matter to the entire university and scientific community. Furthermore, all your academic activities will impact our collective reputation.

Integrity is vital to a university’s reputation

The members of the university live by their reputation. Faculty members are hired and promoted based on their reputation. Students choose which universities to apply to based on their reputation. Institutions are ranked based on their reputation. Graduate schools and employers evaluate prospects based on the university’s reputation. 

Apply Your Understanding 

Question 1:

If you commit an academic integrity violation (AIV) in a course project, could your actions as a student in this one course affect the university’s reputation?  (Select one)

(A) No, I am a single student and can't affect the university's reputation

(B) No, because my reasons for committing a violation are more important

(C) Maybe, but it's not such a big deal for a university with so many successful alums

(D) Yes, because I am also a member of this community. 

Question 2:

One violation is okay because I have time to earn my faculty's trust and work on my credibility  (Select one)

(A) True

(B) False

 

 

Answer to Question 1:

(D) When someone commits a violation and takes a shortcut, they have not actually learned the skills that they were expected to have mastered. Afterwards, anyone who interact with them (at an internship site or during a job interview) can recognize that their skills are limited. Others may form a negative opinion of the quality of our students/graduates and may not think favorably of future candidates from CMU. Remember the Carnegie Mellon Code, one person's actions can certainly affect the community and that includes our reputation.

Answer to Question 2:

(B) False

While it may be that some students make poor decisions that lead to an academic integrity violation, it is important to remember that even one violation can harm the trust between faculty and student and the credibility of a student's work. Relationships with your faculty are key to your academic success as well as your emerging professional network. There is no way to know how much even one integrity related infraction might damage this important relationship. That said, we are all human and we all make mistakes. We may not be able to undo a poor decision or a violation but we can show strength of character by accepting responsibility for our mistakes and seeking to repair the harm in the relationship caused by our choices.  

 

(Content sourced from Professor D. Braiser's OLI course, CMU-Pittsburgh)
